scenes.heading: Data Validation
scenes.narration: Data validation checks incoming data against expectations so bad records are caught before they poison downstream tables.

scenes.heading: What to validate
bullets: Schema: expected columns and data types.
Nullability: required fields are actually present.
Ranges and formats: values make business sense.
Uniqueness and referential integrity across tables.
scenes.narration: Schema checks confirm the shape of the data before anything else. Null and range checks catch missing or nonsensical values, while format checks reject malformed strings. Uniqueness and referential checks ensure keys line up so joins downstream stay trustworthy.

scenes.heading: Where validation fits
scenes.narration: Validation belongs right at the boundary where data enters your system. Records that fail are quarantined rather than dropped silently, so nothing is lost. When failure rates cross a threshold you alert the team, and only data that passes is promoted forward.

scenes.heading: Expressing expectations in code
scenes.code:
import pandera as pa

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({
    "order_id": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.gt(0), unique=True),
    "email":    pa.Column(str, pa.Check.str_matches(r".+@.+\..+")),
    "amount":   pa.Column(float, pa.Check.ge(0)),
})

validated = schema.validate(df, lazy=True)
scenes.narration: This declares the rules the data must satisfy: positive unique order ids, well-formed emails, and non-negative amounts. Running validate checks every row against those rules in one pass. With lazy mode enabled, it collects all failures at once instead of stopping at the first, which speeds up debugging.

scenes.text: Validation enforces schema, nullability, ranges, and integrity at the boundary, quarantining bad rows before they spread.
scenes.narration: Catching bad data at the door is far cheaper than hunting it down after it has contaminated dozens of downstream tables.
